more-pages-from-a-journal: William Hale White, who wrote as Mark Rutherford, continues the spiritual diary begun in his earlier Pages from a Journal. These quiet reflections trace a thoughtful man's wrestling with faith, doubt, and the meaning of an ordinary life. Unadorned and deeply sincere, the entries speak to anyone who has questioned what they were taught to believe.
right-royal: Poet Laureate John Masefield brings his love of the English countryside to this novel of horse racing. At its heart is a great steeplechaser and the people whose hopes ride with him — trainers, owners, and stable lads. Masefield writes of horses with rare understanding, making the racing world vivid even for readers who have never seen a track.
perpetual-light-a-memorial: Poet William Rose Benét — brother of Stephen Vincent Benét — wrote these verses as a memorial to his first wife, who died young. The poems move through grief, remembrance, and quiet faith with tenderness and craft. More than a private elegy, the collection speaks to anyone who has loved and lost.
chaitanya-and-the-vaishnava-poets-of-ben: John Beames brings to English ears Chaitanya, the rapt sixteenth-century holy man of Bengal, and the singers who hymned Krishna in his line. Their songs of godly love stand with India's finest sacred verse. A first-rate scholar's door into Bengal's life of the spirit.
under-the-prophet-in-utah-the-national-m: Frank Cannon, once a Mormon insider and senator, exposes what he calls the political priestcraft of Utah — the church's grip on the state and its citizens. His fierce exposé made him powerful enemies and national headlines. A controversial, revealing blast from the Progressive Era.
john-m-synge-a-few-personal-recollection: John Masefield recalls John Millington Synge — the Playboy of the Western World — with personal warmth. His recollections and notes paint the Irish dramatist vividly. A poet's tribute to a fellow poet. Aran Islands summers and Abbey Theatre nights live in his memoir.
king-coal: Upton Sinclair's King Coal is his blazing novel of Colorado coal miners — their strikes, their suffering, and the tyranny of the companies. His muckraking fiction shook the nation's conscience. A powerful cry for labor justice, as fierce as The Jungle.
